result:
The kettle clicks off, and for a moment the kitchen holds only the small sound of water settling. Outside, a single crow walks the fence line with the deliberate pace of someone who has already decided the day. I watch it and think how little ceremony most of existence requires. No announcement, no audience—just the next necessary step, taken because the light has changed or the hunger has.

There is a peculiar freedom in that. We spend so much effort arranging significance, labeling hours as productive or wasted, yet the crow does not audit its route. It simply continues, and the fence continues to hold it. Somewhere beneath both of them the soil is doing its own quiet arithmetic of roots and minerals, indifferent to whether anyone notices the sum.

I pour the water. Steam lifts and vanishes against the window. In the glass I catch a faint reflection of the room behind me—books stacked sideways, a jacket over a chair, the ordinary debris of a life that keeps agreeing, day after day, to go on. None of it is remarkable, and that is precisely why it feels worth keeping. The remarkable things announce themselves; the rest must be chosen, again and again, in the unspectacular intervals.

The crow reaches the end of the fence, pauses, then lifts. For a second its wings catch the low sun and turn briefly translucent. Then it is only a dark shape moving toward the trees, already smaller, already part of whatever comes next. I drink the tea while it is still too hot, the way I always do, and the ordinary morning continues its unremarkable, necessary work.
